issues.description: PR description and Deepgram docs say control message is {"type":"CloseStream"}, but code sends {"type":"Close"}
issues.detail: The PR title, description, and linked Deepgram SDK reference all state the required control message is {"type": "CloseStream"}. The actual constant _CLOSE_MSG is json.dumps({"type": "Close"}). These are two different values — the server will either ignore the unknown message or fail to flush, which defeats the entire purpose of the fix. The value being sent is the load-bearing fact of this PR; it needs to match the protocol.

issues.description: _close_ws complects three concerns: protocol shutdown, race-condition waiting, and transport close
issues.detail: The new _close_ws is doing three separable things in one method: (1) sending Flush+Close protocol values, (2) waiting on a single receive() as a proxy for 'server caught up', and (3) closing the transport. Each has different failure modes and time semantics. A single receive() with a 1s timeout is a guess, not a protocol — it will return on any inbound frame (an audio chunk, a metadata message) and declare 'we're done'. The 'wait for ack' concern should be a named drain step that reads until a terminal message or timeout, not a one-shot receive.

issues.description: Magic 1.0s timeout and silent TimeoutError are place-oriented constants without a named identity
issues.detail: The 1.0 second budget is an essential piece of behavior (how long we are willing to wait for Deepgram to drain) but it's inlined as a literal. Pull it out as a named constant (or conn_option) so the value has an identity and a reason. Same for the swallowed TimeoutError — at minimum log at debug; the current 'pass' loses the fact that the server did not acknowledge in time, which is exactly the diagnostic you'll want when 429s reappear.

issues.description: Control messages are values; consider colocating with the STT close logic instead of duplicating
issues.detail: _FLUSH_MSG and _CLOSE_MSG are pure data describing a protocol. The PR description notes the STT side already does this correctly. Two copies of the same protocol-shaped data in two files is incidental duplication waiting to drift (this PR is itself evidence — the TTS copy already disagrees with the documented value). A small shared module of Deepgram control-message values would make the protocol a single decomposable fact.

review.summary: The intent of this change is right — the close sequence is a protocol value, not just a TCP close — but the implementation complects protocol shutdown, race-waiting, and transport close in one method, and the load-bearing constant disagrees with the documented Deepgram contract ({\"type\":\"Close\"} vs {\"type\":\"CloseStream\"}). The fix is small: separate the drain step from the close step, name the timeout, and make the control-message values match the spec (ideally shared with the STT side that already gets this right). Essential complexity here is the graceful-shutdown handshake with explicit time semantics; the incidental complexity is the inline literals, the one-shot receive(), and the silent except. Decision: COMPLECTED with one EASY-NOT-SIMPLE wart (the magic 1.0s) and one likely INCIDENTAL bug (wrong message name). Worth merging once the control-message string is corrected and verified against a live Deepgram session.
